nameStory: The Eastern Amberwing gets its name from the stunning amber-colored wings that males display during sunny summer days. The 'eastern' part of the name reflects its original known range, though this little dragonfly has since been found much farther west into central North America. The scientific name 'tenera' means delicate, perfectly capturing this tiny dragonfly's petite and fragile appearance.
description: The Eastern Amberwing is one of New England's tiniest dragonflies, barely reaching an inch in length — small enough to fit comfortably on a quarter! Males are instantly recognizable by their gorgeous amber or orange-tinted wings that glow like stained glass in sunlight. Both males and females sport yellow and brown striped abdomens and bright red wing spots called pterostigmas. This miniature marvel is actually a master of disguise, mimicking wasps to avoid becoming someone's lunch.

idTips.label: Amber Wings (Males)
idTips.description: Males have distinctly orange or amber-colored wings that catch the light beautifully, unlike the clear wings of most dragonflies

idTips.label: Tiny Size
idTips.description: At less than an inch long, this is one of the smallest dragonflies you'll encounter — about the size of a large bee

idTips.label: Red Wing Spots
idTips.description: Both sexes have bright red pterostigmas (small rectangular spots near the wing tips) that stand out against the wing membrane

idTips.label: Striped Abdomen
idTips.description: Yellow and brown banded abdomen creates a wasp-like appearance, especially noticeable when the dragonfly is perched

idTips.label: Wasp-like Behavior
idTips.description: When perched, they wiggle their abdomen and wings in jerky, wasp-like movements — a dead giveaway for identification

idTips.label: Perching Preference
idTips.description: Often perches on low vegetation near water, choosing sunny spots on plant tips or small twigs close to the water's edge

habitat: Eastern Amberwings prefer shallow, warm waters like ponds, slow streams, marshes, and the quiet backwaters of larger rivers. Look for them around cattail marshes, farm ponds, and wetlands with plenty of emergent vegetation. They're particularly fond of areas with muddy or sandy bottoms and abundant aquatic plants where their larvae can develop.

seasonality.spring: Adults begin emerging from their aquatic larval stage in late spring, but numbers are still low. Early spring is spent in the larval stage underwater.
seasonality.summer: Peak flight season runs through summer when males display their amber wings prominently while defending territories. This is the best time to observe their wasp-mimicking behavior and courtship displays.
seasonality.fall: Flight season continues into early fall, though numbers decline as temperatures drop. Late-season individuals may be less vibrant in coloration.
seasonality.winter: Adults die off completely, spending winter as eggs or larvae in the muddy bottoms of ponds and streams.

funFact: This tiny dragonfly is such a convincing wasp impersonator that it actively wiggles its wings and abdomen when perched, putting on a full theatrical performance to trick predators into thinking it has a dangerous stinger!
confusionNotes: The small size and wasp-like appearance might make you think you're looking at an actual wasp at first glance. Remember that dragonflies hold their wings straight out from their body when perched, while wasps fold theirs alongside their body. The large, widely-separated compound eyes are also a dead giveaway that you're looking at a dragonfly.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called 'Eastern' Amberwing, this species actually ranges well into the central United States and even northern Mexico. The name reflects where it was first scientifically described rather than its actual range limits, which is common with many species that were named before their full distribution was understood.
compareHints: The Eastern Amberwing is the only member of its genus in our region, making it fairly distinctive. Among other small dragonflies in the skimmer family, it's unique in having amber-colored wings in males and such pronounced wasp-mimicking behavior. Most other small skimmers have clear wings and lack the distinctive striped abdomen pattern that makes this species look so wasp-like.
